newsitem.title: NORWAY: Fall in ship losses not repeated in 1996 - insurers.
newsitem.headline: Fall in ship losses not repeated in 1996 - insurers.

text.p: The number of ships recorded as total losses continued to decline in 1995 but marine insurers say the picture for 1996 so far does not look so good.

The Institute of London Underwriters (ILU) on Monday said the worldwide total for ships lost in 1995 stands at 109 and, although it will rise as more losses are confirmed, the figure is unlikely to reach the previous year's figure of 119.
However, the ILU said that the improvement has not been maintained in the first half of 1996, with 52 losses recorded by the end of June as against 38 at the same time last year.

The figures, to be presented to delegates at the International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI) conference in Oslo later this week, show the fall in total losses was caused by better experience in bulk shipping, which offset an increase in losses of general cargo ships.

In a note accompanying the statistics, the ILU said, "The slow downward trend in losses by number is readily apparent. However, the decline in losses according to tonnage is more erratic and gives no grounds yet for expecting a continuing fall."
The number of people killed in accidents involving partial or total losses of ships over 500 gross tonnes fell substantially in 1995.
However, this year, with the Tanzanian ferry disaster in May when the Buboka grounded and capsized in Lake Victoria, the total has already reached 730.
The ILU estimates another 500 people have been killed in accidents involving smaller ships from the Philippines, Bangladesh and Indonesia.
